explanations.explanation: I think this one hurts, friend, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't. Look at what comes right after verse 2, though. The text says, “And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob.” Shechem, the prince of the region, doesn't walk away. He stays drawn to her.

Right, he doesn't walk away. The text says, “And his soul was drawn to Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly.” That doesn't wipe out what he did in verse 2, and the text never says it does. It just tells us what Shechem, the prince of the region, felt and did next.

explanations.answer: Get me this girl as a wife
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Shechem tells his father Hamor, “Get me this girl as a wife.” No sneaking around and no mumbling in the corner. He takes it straight to his dad and asks for a marriage.

Nothing in the text has Shechem hushing anything up. He goes to his father Hamor and says it out loud: “Get me this girl as a wife.” Hamor then goes to speak with Jacob, Dinah's father. That's about as far from quiet as you can get.

explanations.answer: Send her back to her father
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what he asks. Shechem wants Dinah to stay, and he tells his father Hamor, “Get me this girl as a wife.” He's asking for a marriage, not a delivery back to Jacob, Dinah's father.

That's what the text says. Jacob heard the news, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, “he remained silent about it until they returned.” I think that was a long wait. Sitting on news like that, with nobody to talk to, is one of the hardest things a person can do.

explanations.answer: Goes to the city gate himself
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't head to the gate. The text says he remained silent until his sons returned from the field. The one who comes to talk is Hamor, who comes to Jacob.

explanations.answer: Packs up the camp to leave
explanations.explanation: No packing here, friend. The text never mentions Jacob breaking camp. It says he “remained silent about it until they returned.” He stays put and waits for his sons.
Yes, fury. The text says Jacob's sons “were filled with grief and fury.” Both of those come together in one verse. This is where the story starts to boil.
Fear isn't the word the text uses. It says they were “filled with grief and fury.” Jacob's sons come in from the field upset and angry, not scared.
The text doesn't say pity. It says Jacob's sons “were filled with grief and fury.” They came in from the field with their sister on their minds, and they were hot about it.
True. The text says Shechem “had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter,” and ends with “…a thing that should not be done.” The text doesn't soften it, and neither will I.
The text is plain about this one, friend. It calls what Shechem did to Dinah an outrage in Israel, and says it is “…a thing that should not be done.” No gray area in that verse.

explanations.answer: To intermarry and settle in the land
explanations.explanation: Yes. Hamor says, “Intermarry with us; give us your daughters and take our daughters for yourselves.” Then he adds, “You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you.” That's a whole package deal: marriage, neighbors and room to grow.

explanations.answer: To leave the region in peace
explanations.explanation: Hamor is offering the opposite of leaving. He says, “You may settle among us, and the land will be open to you.” He's asking Jacob's family to stay, not to go.

explanations.answer: To rule the city alongside him
explanations.explanation: Ruling the city never comes up. What Hamor offers is to intermarry, settle, “move about freely,” and “acquire your own property.” That's a lot of welcome, but a throne isn't in it.

That's it. The brothers say the condition is that “you become circumcised like us,” and then add, “…every one of your males.” Remember, the text already told us they answered deceitfully. Keep that in your back pocket.
The brothers' condition goes well past Shechem. They say, “…every one of your males.” That's a much bigger ask than one man.
Two men is too small a number. The brothers say, “…every one of your males.” That takes in Hamor and Shechem and a lot more.

True. The brothers say, “We will dwell among you and become one people.” Sounds like a happy ending, doesn't it? But the text has already told us they answered deceitfully, so listen to this offer with that in mind.
They do say it. In verse 16 the brothers tell Hamor and Shechem, “We will dwell among you and become one people.” The text has already said they answered deceitfully, so this is part of that answer.

That's what they say. If Hamor's men won't be circumcised, the brothers say, “then we will take our sister and go.” It's the other side of their offer, and it leaves Hamor and Shechem with a choice to make.
The dowry talk comes from Shechem. He tells them to “Demand a high dowry and an expensive gift.” The brothers' answer if the men refuse is different: they say they'll take Dinah and leave.
In this answer it's the sons doing the talking. The text says Jacob's sons answered Shechem and Hamor. If the men refuse, the sons say, “then we will take our sister and go.”

Delighted is the word. The text says Shechem “did not hesitate to fulfill this request, because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter.” That's the reason the text gives, and it's the only one it gives.

Not angry, friend. The text says Shechem “did not hesitate to fulfill this request,” and gives the reason: “…because he was delighted with Jacob's daughter.” The brothers' condition didn't make him mad.
The text says the opposite of uneasy. Shechem “did not hesitate,” because “he was delighted with Jacob's daughter.” No second-guessing at all.
They say the opposite. Hamor and Shechem tell the men at the gate, “These men are at peace with us.” They're selling this as good news. And they have no idea what the brothers are really planning.

False, and you've got it. At the gate, Hamor and Shechem say, “These men are at peace with us. Let them live and trade in our land.” They present Jacob's family as friends. They don't know the brothers answered deceitfully.
True. They ask the men at the gate, “Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours?” That's part of the pitch. They tell the men what they have to gain.
They do say it, friend. In verse 23 they ask, “Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours?” It's part of how they make their case to the men of the city.
Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers. The text names them right there in verse 25. This is a heavy part of the story, friend, so let's take it slow.
Reuben and Judah are sons of Jacob (Genesis 35:23), but the text doesn't name them here. It names Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, as the two who take their swords.
Gad and Asher are sons of Jacob too (Genesis 35:26), but they aren't the pair in this verse. The text names Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers. The other sons only show up later in the passage.
Yes, Dinah. The text says they “took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went away.” She's the one they came for, and she's the one the text names.
No servants in this verse. The text says Simeon and Levi “took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went away.” Dinah is the only person it names.
Elders don't come into it here. Verse 26 says they “took Dinah out of Shechem's house.” She's the one they take with them.

True. Verse 27 says Jacob's other sons “came upon the slaughter and looted the city,” and then gives the reason: “…because their sister had been defiled.” That's the text's reason for it. Heavy stuff, friend.
The text does say it. Jacob's other sons looted the city, “…because their sister had been defiled.” The reason is right there in verse 27.
Children. The text says they “carried off all their possessions and women and children.” That's a heavy line, friend, and I think it's meant to be.
Elders aren't the word in verse 29. The text says they “carried off all their possessions and women and children.” The word you want is children.
Warriors aren't mentioned in that verse. It says they “carried off all their possessions and women and children.” The word you want is children.
That's Jacob's fear. He says, “We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.” He's counting heads, and the numbers don't look good to him.

explanations.answer: Drive his flocks out of Canaan
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't say anything about his flocks being driven out. He says, “if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.” His worry is about an attack.

explanations.answer: Refuse to trade with his family
explanations.explanation: Trade isn't what Jacob is worried about. His words are, “if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed.” That's a much bigger fear than a closed market.

explanations.answer: They ask if Shechem should have treated their sister like a prostitute
explanations.explanation: That's their answer. They reply, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” They don't say sorry and they don't promise anything. They answer their father with a question.

explanations.answer: They say they are sorry for the trouble they caused
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give us an apology. After Jacob speaks, Simeon and Levi reply, “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” Their answer is a question, and it's all the text gives us from them.

explanations.answer: They promise to make peace with the people of the land
explanations.explanation: No peace promise shows up in the text. Simeon and Levi answer Jacob with a question: “Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?” That's the last word the passage gives them.
